\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{صهر} (ṣihr)}{صهر (ṣihr)}]{\ar{صهر} (ṣihr) — a son-in-law; a brother-in-law}

\label{lesson:AR-C529-sihr}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for single, then the Arabic for to love passionately.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{صهر}}
\textbf{\ar{صهر}} — \emph{ṣihr} — \textquotedblleft{}a son-in-law; a brother-in-law\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{ساعد} \ar{صهري} \ar{أبي} \ar{في} \ar{نقل} \ar{الأثاث}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{sāʿada ṣihrī abī fī naql al-athāth.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My son-in-law helped my father move the furniture.
\end{quote}

Plural: \ar{أصهار}, \emph{aṣhār}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{صهر}} (\emph{ṣihr}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ṣ-h-r}, \textquotedblleft{}kinship by marriage\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives ṣihr as a relation by marriage.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṣihr}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṣihr}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sāʿada ṣihrī abī fī naql al-athāth.} — My son-in-law helped my father move the furniture.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for single, then the Arabic for to love passionately, then say \emph{ṣihr} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{صهر} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A son-in-law; a brother-in-law\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{كنة} (kanna)}{كنة (kanna)}]{\ar{كنة} (kanna) — a daughter-in-law}

\label{lesson:AR-C529-kanna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to love passionately, then the Arabic for a son-in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{كنة}}
\textbf{\ar{كنة}} — \emph{kanna} — \textquotedblleft{}a daughter-in-law\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{تحب} \ar{جدتي} \ar{كنتها} \ar{كثيرا}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tuḥibbu jaddatī kannatahā kathīran.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My grandmother loves her daughter-in-law very much.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{كنة}} (\emph{kanna}) is an old native Arabic word for a son's or a brother's wife, usually traced to the root \emph{k-n-n}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover, to shelter\textquotedblright{}; how the sense grew is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kanna}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kanna}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tuḥibbu jaddatī kannatahā kathīran.} — My grandmother loves her daughter-in-law very much.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to love passionately, then the Arabic for a son-in-law, then say \emph{kanna} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{كنة} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A daughter-in-law\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{نسيب} (nasīb)}{نسيب (nasīb)}]{\ar{نسيب} (nasīb) — an in-law}

\label{lesson:AR-C529-nasib}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a son-in-law, then the Arabic for a daughter-in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{نسيب}}
\textbf{\ar{نسيب}} — \emph{nasīb} — \textquotedblleft{}an in-law\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{جاء} \ar{نسيبي} \ar{لزيارتنا} \ar{في} \ar{العيد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{jāʾa nasībī li-ziyāratinā fī al-ʿīd.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My in-law came to visit us at the feast.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{نسيب}} (\emph{nasīb}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{n-s-b}, \textquotedblleft{}lineage, relationship\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Nasab, lineage, is from the same root: a nasīb is kin by marriage.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nasīb}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nasīb}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jāʾa nasībī li-ziyāratinā fī al-ʿīd.} — My in-law came to visit us at the feast.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a son-in-law, then the Arabic for a daughter-in-law, then say \emph{nasīb} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{نسيب} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}An in-law\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{عديل} (ʿadīl)}{عديل (ʿadīl)}]{\ar{عديل} (ʿadīl) — a brother-in-law (by sisters)}

\label{lesson:AR-C529-adil}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a daughter-in-law, then the Arabic for an in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{عديل}}
\textbf{\ar{عديل}} — \emph{ʿadīl} — \textquotedblleft{}a brother-in-law (by sisters)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{عديلي} \ar{متزوج} \ar{من} \ar{أخت} \ar{زوجتي}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ʿadīlī mutazawwij min ukht zawjatī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My brother-in-law is married to my wife's sister.
\end{quote}

Two men married to two sisters are \ar{عديلان}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عديل}} (\emph{ʿadīl}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-d-l}, \textquotedblleft{}to be equal, to be fair\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives ʿadīl as an equal, a counterpart; the sense of two men with sisters for wives is usually explained from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ʿadīl}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ʿadīl}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ʿadīlī mutazawwij min ukht zawjatī.} — My brother-in-law is married to my wife's sister.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a daughter-in-law, then the Arabic for an in-law, then say \emph{ʿadīl} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{عديل} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A brother-in-law (by sisters)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{طلاق} (ṭalāq)}{طلاق (ṭalāq)}]{\ar{طلاق} (ṭalāq) — a marriage break-up; a divorce}

\label{lesson:AR-C529-talaq}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for an in-law, then the Arabic for a brother-in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{طلاق}}
\textbf{\ar{طلاق}} — \emph{ṭalāq} — \textquotedblleft{}a marriage break-up; a divorce\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{بعد} \ar{الطلاق} \ar{سكن} \ar{صديقي} \ar{وحده}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{baʿda aṭ-ṭalāq sakana ṣadīqī waḥdahu.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
After the divorce my friend lived alone.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{طلاق}} (\emph{ṭalāq}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ṭ-l-q}, \textquotedblleft{}to be free, to be let go\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Ṭalāq is the letting go of a marriage.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭalāq}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭalāq}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{baʿda aṭ-ṭalāq sakana ṣadīqī waḥdahu.} — After the divorce my friend lived alone.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for an in-law, then the Arabic for a brother-in-law, then say \emph{ṭalāq} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{طلاق} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A marriage break-up; a divorce\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
